Always Tired, but Your Blood Work Is Normal?

By Adam Seay, D.C., Root Health, Garner, NC. Updated October 2, 2026.

The short answer

A standard panel is built to catch serious disease, and it does that reasonably well. It was not built to tell you whether your iron stores, B12, thyroid conversion, blood sugar, stress hormone rhythm or sleep are good enough for you to feel well. "Normal" usually means nothing alarming showed up. It does not mean nothing is there.

You are in bed seven or eight hours. Your labs came back normal. The advice was to manage your stress, or maybe to try an antidepressant. And you are still tired in a way a good night or a second coffee does not touch. Fatigue is the most common complaint that walks into my office, and it is also the one most likely to be waved off, because nothing on a basic panel looks bad enough to act on.

Fatigue like this is rarely one problem. It is usually several smaller ones stacking up. These are the ones I see missed most.

Six things a standard panel can miss

1. Low iron stores without anemia

A complete blood count catches anemia. It does not catch iron stores that are low but not yet low enough to drop your hemoglobin. In a randomized trial of menstruating women with a ferritin under 50 and no anemia, fatigue fell about 48 percent with oral iron against 29 percent with placebo.1 Many labs still call that ferritin normal.

2. B12 that looks fine but is not working

A serum B12 can sit inside the range while your cells are short. Methylmalonic acid rises when B12 is not doing its job at the cell level, so it is worth asking for alongside the B12 itself.

3. Thyroid beyond TSH

Subclinical hypothyroidism affects up to one in ten adults, and fatigue, foggy thinking and low mood are common with it.2 A TSH is a screening test. Free T3, the active hormone, and reverse T3, which rises under stress and illness, fill in what it cannot show. More on that in Normal TSH, but still feel hypothyroid?

4. Blood sugar swings

Fasting glucose and A1c are useful but late. Fasting insulin tends to catch insulin resistance years before glucose drifts out of range. Swings matter too: every crash after a spike triggers a cortisol and adrenaline response to bring glucose back up, which adds to the stress load below.

5. A stress hormone rhythm that is off

Healthy cortisol runs high in the morning and low at night. In chronic fatigue, research has documented lower cortisol output and a flatter daily curve.3 A single morning blood draw says little about a rhythm, so I use a four-point test across the day. A flat, low curve and a wired, high one can feel similar and need different handling. To be clear, this is not "adrenal fatigue." That is not a recognized diagnosis, and I do not use it. The test is about the shape of the curve.

6. Sleep that does not repair

Eight hours in bed is not the same as eight hours of deep, restoring sleep. Poor sleep drives low-grade inflammation, and inflammation makes sleep worse.4 For long-running insomnia, the best-studied treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, a short structured program that improved sleep across objective and diary measures in a major review.5 Loud snoring or waking up gasping is a separate question for a sleep study.

If you crash a day or two after effort, read this. If physical or mental exertion leaves you much worse a day or two later, that pattern is called post-exertional malaise, and it is a hallmark of ME/CFS. In ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, the rise in pain after exercise is larger when it is measured 8 to 72 hours afterward than right away.6 Pushing through to rebuild stamina can set you back. Pacing, staying inside the amount you can do without a crash, is where to start, and it is worth sorting out before anyone hands you an exercise program.

What to ask your doctor for

  • CBC and a comprehensive metabolic panel
  • Ferritin and iron studies
  • B12 with methylmalonic acid, and folate
  • Vitamin D (25-OH)
  • TSH, free T4, free T3, reverse T3 and thyroid antibodies
  • Fasting glucose, A1c and fasting insulin
  • hs-CRP, a general marker of inflammation

If those come back clean and you still feel this way, the next layer is more specialized. It should be chosen by your pattern, not ordered all at once.

Common questions

Can low ferritin cause fatigue if I am not anemic?

Yes. In the randomized trial above, non-anemic women with a ferritin under 50 had a larger drop in fatigue on iron than on placebo. Iron can also be overdone, so supplement based on a level, not a guess.

Is adrenal fatigue real?

Not as a diagnosis. It is not recognized, and I do not use the term. What is real is that the daily cortisol rhythm can be measurably off, especially in chronic fatigue, and a four-point test across the day shows it.

What if all my tests really are normal?

Then the pattern matters more than any single number: when the fatigue started, what makes it worse, whether you crash after effort, and what else travels with it. That is what the free quiz and a Discovery Session are for.
